All they need to do is arrange the fish into different patterns, which earn them points depending on how complex the pattern is. In addition, once all the displays are filled, the players score extra points based on the number of bettas of their color in each of the displays. Try Betta on BGA to discover 2 of its game modes (classic and solo) and explore their different strategies. Discover the third game mode (asymmetric) by playing the physical version. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Set-up 3 Gameplay 4 Game end 5 Final scoring 6 Solo mode Overview In Betta, players are tasked with arranging displays of bettas in Betty’s pet shop, scoring points for making certain patterns, and for the amount of their own coloured bettas there are in the final displays. The main description below is for 2–4 players. For solo mode, see the section at the end. Set-up Each player starts with a hand of 3 cards, and a stack of 6 face-down cards. Each card shows two bettas of the player’s colour, and one of another colour. Across the middle of the screen are a number of displays (5, 6 or 8, depending on the number of players). Some of these displays will already have three bettas in them: for each player there is a display with a card of that player’s type in it. At the top of the screen are shown the target patterns (which vary from game to game). (There are reports that sometimes these patterns are not displayed. If this happens, try hitting F5 to do a browser refresh.) Gameplay On each of their turns, a player chooses a card from their hand, optionally rotates it by a multiple of 90°, and places it on a display of their choice, except that it is not allowed to play on a display that already has 9 visible bettas. If placing the card produces one of the target patterns, in bettas of a single colour, then the player scores 3, 5 or 7 points, as indicated above the pattern in question. If the move makes more than one pattern, only the one that would score the most counts. In order to be considered to match a target pattern: • The pattern needs to be formed by bettas of a single colour, but this does not have to be the player’s own colour. • It does not matter if there are extra bettas of the same colour that are not part of the pattern. • The pattern does not need to be in the orientation shown at the top of the screen — any rotation of that pattern counts. • It does not matter if the pattern was already present before the player played the new card, as long as at least one of bettas in the pattern comes from that card. Playing a card into an empty display cannot produce one of the target patterns, but scores 2 points anyway. Having played a card, the player receives another card from their stack, if the stack is not empty. Game end The game ends when either of the following occurs: • All displays have 9 visible bettas. • All players have taken 7 turns (and therefore have only two cards remaining in hand). Final scoring At the end of the game each player scores points for the number of bettas of their colour visible in the displays, according to the table shown below their hand: 0 points for less than 2 bettas, 1 point for 2 bettas, 3 points for 3 bettas, 6 points for 4 bettas, 10 points for 5 bettas, and 15 points for 6 or more bettas. These points are scored for each display individually, and are added to the previously scored points to produce the player’s final score. The winner is the player with the highest score. If two or more players are tied on the highest score, then victory goes to the player with the most visible bettas of their colour, or if that fails to break the tie, then to the player with the most visible bettas of their colour in a single display; if that too fails to break the tie, then the game is a tie. [Rating: 1/10] Simple game of pattern matching.  Colourful, not terrible but nothing compelling.

[Rating: 1/10] [b]Pattern placement reduced to decorative bookkeeping.[/b] Arrange fish, chase scoring patterns, and occasionally interfere with an opponent’s display. The visual puzzle is pleasant enough, but the choices are thin, the incentives obvious, and the experience feels closer to completing a worksheet than navigating a game. Attractive, harmless, and almost entirely disposable.

[Rating: 2/10] The rare case of a game being more fun to play on BGA than it is in person - the 3x3 cards were an interesting idea, but in practice they get caught on each other too easily, and sleeving them would be a massive gameplay detriment.   Even so, this game devolves quickly at 2 players, my usual player count, into "whoever scores a decent point while simultaneously blocking the opponent" first wins. After a few games in a row with nearly identical low 20s to low teens scores, I gave up. [Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  It works just fine as a quick playing filler where you try to make certain patterns for points. Just didn't do much for me.

[Rating: 3/10] At least it's short.  Found it incredibly frustrating as I watched other players actually have cards that could earn them points and I was able to achieve maybe two or three scores at most.  I had more endgame points than in game points.  I'd rather play something like Canvas.

[Rating: 3/10] Game where you lay transparent cards to try and match up spaces on common tiles. It is surprisingly decent in many ways - particularly in the fact that it is meaningfully interactive, but the core idea is not solid enough to carry the experience and keeping you wanting to come back

[Rating: 3/10] it's basically just visual pattern recognition on some 3x3 grids, with static objectives (no, they don't even change during the game). yeah, there's a bit of area control or w/e at the end but it's so basic that you barely feel that.

[Rating: 4/10] Lightweight "card laying" game for the families. Not that much game included, unfortunately.
